newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Human rights champion mourned in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Human rights champion mourned in Cambodia.

text.p: Several hundred Cambodians attended the funeral on Thursday of a human rights worker who survived the horrors of Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge "killing fields" regime in the 1970s only to meet a brutal death in Rwanda.
Unidentified assassins killed 34-year-old Chim-Chan Sastra and three other U.N. human rights monitors, a Briton and two Rwandans, in an ambush on February 4 in southwestern Rwanda.
"Cambodia definitely can't afford to lose people like this,' said Brad Adams, his former employer in the legal department of the Phnom Penh-based U.N. Centre for Human Rights (UNCHR).
"It's tragic for him, his family and the country because if the country ever develops you'd hope to see him as a leader of the country," he said.

Chim-Chan Sastra survived the brutal 1975-79 rule of the Khmer Rouge, when more than one million people are estimated to have died of execution, starvation, disease or overwork, and fled to Thailand when the Vietnamese took over the country in 1979.
In the ensuing civil war, Chim-Chan Sastra led a battalion of 500 soldiers as one of the youngest commanders of the non-communist Khmer People's National Liberation Front faction.
Chim-Chan Sastra won a scholarship in 1989 for human rights studies at Columbia University in the United States. He returned home in 1994 to join the UNCHR.
He joined the opposition Khmer Nation Party, left for Rwanda as a U.N. Volunteer last year and was due to return to his UNCHR job in Phnom Penh on March 3.
